A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GPG research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original GPG training and evaluation results for mathematical reasoning and multimodal tasks, plus group-size and reward-normalization ablations in Tables 2–10.

after.justification: V4 retains original empirical results and reports additional method ablations, a DAPO comparison, general-capability evaluations, and results with uncertainty estimates.

M1.justification: V1 uses group-standard-deviation-normalized advantages and an unscaled policy-gradient loss. V4 makes normalization optional, uses unnormalized centered rewards in its final variant, and introduces AGE scaling by alpha = B/(B−M). Algorithm 1 additionally accumulates and resamples responses until a minimum valid-sample proportion is reached. These change the optimization and sampling procedure.

E1.justification: V4 retains the original mathematics and multimodal coverage while adding MMLU, Chinese C-Eval, MBPP/MBPP+, HellaSwag, and TruthfulQA evaluations. These extend coverage to general knowledge, Chinese disciplinary questions, coding, and general QA. It also adds training on the DAPO data source for the new 7B experiment.

E2.justification: DAPO moves from a discussed algorithm in v1 to an evaluated comparator in v4 Table 9. The expanded 7B comparison adds OpenReasoner-Zero and SimpleRL-Zero, among others. Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct disappears, while rStar-Math and Eurus are retained in the reorganized 7B table. Existing GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and multimodal comparisons remain.

E3.justification: V4 adds a 7B training protocol and DAPO comparison controlling the training dataset and 1,100 training steps, with GPG using accuracy-only rewards. It adds pass@3/pass@5 evaluation on four mathematics benchmarks, OpenCompass general-knowledge evaluation, and zero-shot coding/QA testing. The original 1.5B training budgets of 100 and 50 steps remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V4 adds ablations separating normalization, AGE, and resampling effects; threshold sensitivity tests; and diagnostics of reward dispersion and zero-gradient groups (Tables 1, 10, 15 and Figure 2). It also tests preservation of general capabilities. Original group-size results, training curves, and the case study are retained. Conversely, v1's numerical KL-penalty ablation disappears despite its discussion remaining.

E5.justification: V1 provides no explicit repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. V4 Table 16 reports accuracy and standard deviation, with its caption specifying four random seeds, and Table 19 reports standard errors for HellaSwag and TruthfulQA. This establishes substantially expanded uncertainty reporting, without establishing an increase from a known earlier run count or four independent retrainings.

E6.justification: Reported GPG results change from 69.11 to 76.15 on CV-Bench, 50.80 to 51.33 on GEOQA, and 86.0 to 89.0 average classification accuracy; LISA validation mIoU falls from 53.4 to 51.3. V4 adds general-task, repeated-evaluation, and resource-cost results. Its new GPG-Zero-7B average of 57.7 uses the DAPO-data setting and is not a same-setting gain over v1's 45.3. The 1.5B averages of 55.7 and 55.5 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: V4 introduces formal gradient-scaling definitions and derivations in Equations 7–8 and a new distributed-averaging analysis in Appendix A. The latter derives the relationship between averaging over all samples and averaging over nonzero-gradient samples. V1 has no corresponding analysis. Its existing PPO/GRPO derivations are retained in v4 Appendix C.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add correction of advantage and gradient-estimation biases, AGE, and variance-reducing resampling as central contributions. The headline performance claim broadens from outperforming GRPO to achieving state-of-the-art results. The original claims of simplifying reinforcement learning by removing critic/reference models and distributional constraints remain.

C2.justification: V4 reinterprets standard-deviation normalization as introducing reward bias while incidentally providing gradient correction, replacing v1's straightforward variance-reduction justification. It adds discussion of high variance when valid samples are scarce, DAPO sampling inefficiency, and preservation of general capabilities. The limitation concerning unevaluated extremely large models is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies VERL, 144 prompts per batch, eight responses per prompt, AdamW, learning rate 1e−6, weight decay 0.1, threshold 0.6, 1,100 steps, and 48 NPUs for the added 7B experiment. V4 also supplies a dedicated 7B prompt and reproducibility statement. The project link already existed; v1's explicit 7,500-sample MATH-lighteval disclosure is no longer included.

R1.justification: V4 substantially develops its positioning against Dr. GRPO and DAPO: it disputes the benefit of removing normalization alone and argues that AGE avoids costs of constructing fully valid batches. This extends v1's primarily simplification-based positioning. References expand to OpenReasoner-Zero, SimpleRL, VERL, C-Eval, and recent reasoning-RL applications, while several older references are removed.

P1.justification: V4 moves Related Work after the experiments, reorganizes mathematical evaluation around distilled 1.5B and base 7B models, and transfers prompts, several ablations, training curves, and the case study into structured appendices. It adds a reproducibility section and substantially revises the introduction's motivation and method exposition, alongside widespread language editing.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned into separate mathematics and multimodal panels, and a new diagnostic Figure 2 is added. The original training curves and case illustration are reused in the appendix. Mathematical comparison tables are reorganized, and new component, resource, uncertainty, and general-benchmark tables are introduced. The conference layout also substantially compresses some tables, especially classification results.

improvement.justification: V1 claims computational efficiency without quantitative resource comparisons and supplies no explicit uncertainty estimates. V4 adds a comparison controlling dataset and training steps with DAPO, measured resource costs, component ablations, broader evaluations, uncertainty reporting, and concrete training configurations. These substantially strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. There are material weaknesses: the KL-ablation evidence disappears, and Appendix A establishes a rescaling identity rather than proving unbiasedness for the original RL objective. Nevertheless, the gains in evaluability and supporting evidence constitute a substantial overall improvement.
